title: Two Weeks

jokes.text: Michael recounting his resignation story in agonizing, meandering detail — starting with needing to pee on the drive
jokes.setup: Michael is about to tell the dramatic story of how he quit his job — the office is hanging on every word
jokes.punchline: He buries the lede with irrelevant details: 'Two hours to go. Feeling good. Crank some tunes. Should've peed before I left.'
jokes.explanation: A beautifully character-specific opener. Michael's inability to tell a story efficiently is his defining trait, and burying 'should've peed before I left' in his triumphant quitting story is perfectly him. Strong structure: we have maximum anticipation, and he deflates it with maximum mundanity.

jokes.text: Michael walked into the wrong building due to nerves
jokes.setup: After the meandering setup, the group finally gets Michael to focus: 'You're in the right building, you're with the right people — what happened?'
jokes.punchline: Revelation that all the meandering detail was even worse: he went to the wrong building first
jokes.explanation: A solid escalation on the storytelling-incompetence joke. The wrong-building detail adds a layer of pathetic incompetence to what should be Michael's finest hour. Works because it's specific and believable for the character.

jokes.text: 'He finally has a story we really wanna hear. And he knows it.'
jokes.setup: Michael is drawing out the quitting story to maximum effect
jokes.punchline: Jim's talking-head commentary cuts to the core of Michael's narrative manipulation — he's milking it
jokes.explanation: Tight, economical Jim talking-head. Two sentences that perfectly diagnose Michael's behavior and the dynamic of the scene. The 'and he knows it' kicker is the right length — one beat past the obvious observation, landing with a knowing precision.

jokes.text: 'You have no idea how high I can fly.'
jokes.setup: Michael delivers his dramatic resignation to David Wallace
jokes.punchline: His supposedly epic parting line is grandiose but vague and slightly absurd — 'how high I can fly'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines. It's quintessentially Michael: he thinks he's delivering a devastating power move, but the metaphor is barely coherent. 'You have no idea how high I can fly' is simultaneously inspirational-poster empty and weirdly poignant. Very high character integration — no other character on TV could deliver this line sincerely.

jokes.text: The coworkers' fantasy quitting-speech suggestions: 'Wouldn't it feel good to tell him he's incompetent... that he's wasted 15 years of your life? Maybe spit in his face?'
jokes.setup: Michael describes his dignified exit; coworkers are surprised he didn't rage
jokes.punchline: The escalating suggestions (incompetent → wasted your life → spit in his face) reveal how much the staff has fantasized about quitting themselves
jokes.explanation: The escalation to 'maybe spit in his face?' is a well-earned surprise. The joke structure builds from reasonable (tell him he's incompetent) to darkly personal (wasted 15 years) to absurdly physical (spitting). Also reveals character: these people have spent more time planning the speech than Michael did.

jokes.text: 'You guys have thought about this a lot more than I have. I just winged it.'
jokes.setup: Coworkers deliver increasingly elaborate quitting-speech fantasies
jokes.punchline: Michael's oblivious non-reaction exposes that the coworkers are projecting their own repressed workplace rage
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff on joke #5. Michael's breezy obliviousness turns the joke back around: the people who couldn't quit are the ones who've rehearsed the speech. Clean, economic, character-true.

jokes.text: 'I love a good quitting story. It makes me feel like I have control over my own life. Gives me hope. Maybe I'll have one of my own someday. But I dream.'
jokes.setup: Michael's quitting story captivates the office
jokes.punchline: Pam's talking-head reveals her quitting fantasy — then deflates it with 'but I dream' — suggesting she's fully resigned to her own captivity
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best early joke and one of the series' best Pam talking-heads. The irony is rich: Pam will actually quit by the end of this episode, making 'but I dream' a tragic setup she doesn't know is a setup. 'But I dream' as the kicker — delivered flatly — perfectly encapsulates the existential dread of being stuck in a bad job. High on all craft metrics: original, economical, deeply character-specific (especially given her arc), and earned through years of buildup.

jokes.text: 'There is a very big difference between Michael trying and Michael not trying.'
jokes.setup: Jim's talking-head notes that Michael gave his two weeks' notice a week ago
jokes.punchline: The understated observation implies Michael's 'trying' version was already barely functional, so 'not trying' must be spectacular
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical setup for the act to follow. The line works as a premise-establisher and as a standalone joke — what follows (scotch and Splenda at his desk) is the visual punchline. Jim's flat delivery would make this land beautifully.

jokes.text: 'Scotch and Splenda. Tastes like Splenda, gets drunk like Scotch.'
jokes.setup: Jim catches Michael drinking at his desk and asks if it's Scotch
jokes.punchline: Michael's invented cocktail description ('Tastes like Splenda, gets drunk like Scotch') is both nutritionally confused and deeply sad
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top-tier jokes. 'Tastes like Splenda, gets drunk like Scotch' is a brilliantly absurd construction — it implies he's trying to be health-conscious while drinking at work, which captures Michael's delusion perfectly. The parallel structure ('tastes like X, gets drunk like Y') is textbook comedic economy. It's quotable, original, and absolutely could not come from any other character. Strong contender for the episode's best line.

jokes.text: Michael's 'last days' declaration: 'I'm gonna stay up all day. I'm gonna sleep up all night.'
jokes.setup: Michael announces his lax new attitude now that he's leaving
jokes.punchline: 'Sleep up all night' — an unintentional malapropism suggesting Michael can't even get his rebel manifesto right
jokes.explanation: The inverted phrase 'sleep up all night' is subtle but effective — Michael reverses the idiom, suggesting he can't even correctly articulate his own rebellion. Could be intentional absurdism or a character-true verbal stumble. Either reading works.

jokes.text: Michael insists he'll be 'headhunted' for a new job rather than look for one
jokes.setup: Pam suggests Michael should be making calls about jobs since he has only four days left
jokes.punchline: Michael insists 'at my level, you don't just look in the want ads' — he'll be headhunted — revealing complete delusion about his marketability
jokes.explanation: Solid character joke about Michael's inflated self-image. Functional and true to the character, but not especially original — Michael's delusion about his professional stature is a well-worn vein.

jokes.text: 'Any really good headhunter will storm your village at sunset with overwhelming force and cut off your head with a ceremonial knife.'
jokes.setup: Pam presses: 'Have you called any headhunters?' Michael says any good headhunter already knows he's available
jokes.punchline: Michael extends the 'headhunter' metaphor to its violent literal conclusion with bizarre specificity ('ceremonial knife,' 'at sunset')
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist joke. Taking the word 'headhunter' to its tribal, literal extreme — complete with 'ceremonial knife' and 'at sunset' — is a well-constructed bit of wordplay that escalates to just the right level of bizarre. The specificity ('ceremonial' knife, not just any knife) is what elevates it from decent to very good. Pam's deadpan 'Right, 'cause that's what we're talking about' is the perfect button.

jokes.text: 'You can talk to me for as long as you want, because I have all the time in the world.' / 'Oh, God.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis asks to talk to Michael for a minute
jokes.punchline: Michael's generous offer and Phyllis's immediate 'Oh, God' — she didn't want a long conversation, just a quick farewell
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional gag. Phyllis's 'Oh, God' is the joke — she came to do something nice and immediately regrets it. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael already has wine at his desk, and Phyllis's farewell wine is redundant
jokes.setup: Phyllis brings a bottle of wine as a farewell gift
jokes.punchline: Michael reveals he's already drinking wine — the gift is unnecessary because he's pre-loaded
jokes.explanation: Efficient visual gag. The reveal that Michael is already drinking — compounding the earlier Scotch-and-Splenda — paints a portrait of a man in complete professional freefall. Works as escalation in a minor key.

jokes.text: The job candidate in the waiting room asks Dwight if he's also interviewing — Dwight says yes, then Charles announces he's going with an outside hire 'for obvious reasons'
jokes.setup: A job candidate assumes Dwight is also interviewing for the regional manager position
jokes.punchline: Dwight claims he is — then Charles announces they're going outside 'for obvious reasons,' humiliating Dwight without even addressing him
jokes.explanation: 'For obvious reasons' is doing a lot of work here — it's a devastating, casual dismissal of Dwight's ambitions without Charles even needing to look at him. The gag is structurally excellent: candidate assumes → Dwight inflates → Charles deflates publicly. High character integration for both Dwight's eternal ambition and Charles's contempt.

jokes.text: Kevin presses Pam about the copier — 'Soon could mean anything. Soon could be three weeks. Is that what soon means to you?' / 'Sometimes.' / 'Then come back soon.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is impatient about the copier being ready; Pam says it'll be ready 'soon'
jokes.punchline: Kevin philosophically deconstructs 'soon,' Pam concedes it could mean three weeks, so Kevin uses her own word against her as a dismissal
jokes.explanation: Underrated gem. Kevin — normally played as dim — applies incisive logic to the word 'soon' and uses Pam's own admission to dismiss her. 'Then come back soon' is a perfect button: unexpected wit from an unexpected source. The joke subverts Kevin's characterization, which earns a bonus for originality. Well-structured, economical, and surprisingly quotable.

jokes.text: 'Bandit, no! No, no, no!' — a cat apparently loose in the office
jokes.setup: The chaos of copier installation; Angela's cat Bandit is apparently present in the office
jokes.punchline: The absurdity of a cat being loose during the copier chaos
jokes.explanation: Functional Angela character beat — she has a cat in the office, which is on-brand — but as a pure audio moment without visual support it's thin. Works mainly as a character texture moment rather than a proper joke.

jokes.text: Pam's confessional about the copier: 'Yesterday they delivered the new one. But they didn't set it up. So my day just got a little more interesting.'
jokes.setup: The copier saga has been established. Pam explains the situation.
jokes.punchline: 'So my day just got a little more interesting' — massive understatement about what is clearly a nightmare, delivered with Pam's trademark dry affect.
jokes.explanation: Pam's dry self-deprecation is consistent with her character. Functional joke, not a standout, but it's economical and character-appropriate.

jokes.text: 'It's monster.com. Singular. Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Michael (presumably) is looking for jobs and getting the website wrong
jokes.punchline: Pam has to correct him that it's 'monster.com' not 'monsters.com' — Michael is so clueless he can't even Google himself a job
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient joke about Michael's helplessness. The 'singular' correction is understated and a bit arch — it implies he's been trying monsters.com (or some variation). Works as a minor character beat.

jokes.text: Prince Paper's voicemail: 'We are sad to inform you that after 40 years of serving the community, we are no longer in business... Bye!'
jokes.setup: Michael, researching competitors, calls Prince Paper — a family business his scheming previously helped destroy
jokes.punchline: The cheerful 'Bye!' at the end of a somber closure message; also the dark callback that Michael's actions ended this company
jokes.explanation: The cheerful 'Bye!' tacked onto a somber 40-year closure message is darkly funny on its own. For viewers who watched 'Prince Family Paper,' the moment is gut-punch dark comedy — Michael helped destroy this business and is now accidentally calling its ghost. The juxtaposition of chipper sign-off with devastating content is sharp. Bonus for the moral weight it brings.

jokes.text: Michael asks Jim to close his eyes before revealing his big idea — Jim refuses and says 'it added nothing' when Michael insists
jokes.setup: Michael dramatically asks Jim to close his eyes before the big reveal
jokes.punchline: Jim refuses, Michael insists, Jim concedes — then when Michael says 'close them,' Jim's 'it added nothing' is the perfect dry editorial on Michael's theatrical instincts
jokes.explanation: 'It added nothing' is Jim at his deadpan best — a precise, devastating small critique of Michael's performative style. The escalating negotiation over whether to close his eyes is also a good structural setup for the reveal.

jokes.text: 'Do you know the industry's in decline?' / 'Yeah. Oh, God, I practically invented decline.'
jokes.setup: Jim challenges Michael's paper company plan by noting the industry is declining
jokes.punchline: Michael's response — 'I practically invented decline' — is meant as self-deprecation but accidentally reveals deep self-awareness (or total confusion about what he's admitting)
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'I practically invented decline' is a masterpiece of accidental self-awareness — Michael thinks he's deflecting, but he's accurately describing his own career trajectory. The line is funny, quotable, dark, and layered. You can read it as Michael being weirdly honest or completely deluded — and both readings are funny. Economy is perfect: four words, loaded with meaning.

jokes.text: 'What I wish for you is that you land a job at a company that A, exists, and B, has a salary'
jokes.setup: Jim declines to join Michael's paper company
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'wish' for Michael sets the floor at 'the company should exist' — a devastatingly low bar that implies Michael can't even clear it
jokes.explanation: Sharp Jim line. The joke is structural: Jim lowers the bar so far ('A, exists') that clearing it would already be impressive, which indicts Michael's plan without any direct insult. The list format ('A... B...') gives it the feel of a formal assessment, which makes the absurdity of the criteria funnier. Highly quotable and reusable out of context.

jokes.text: Charles asks Jim if he also handed in his notice; Jim says no — 'Okay.' / 'After you.' / 'No, I'm staying.' / 'Okay.'
jokes.setup: Charles, suspicious, corners Jim about whether he's also quitting
jokes.punchline: The clipped exchange — 'After you.' / 'No, I'm staying.' / 'Okay.' — is a masterclass in awkward professional tension played for dry laughs
jokes.explanation: The economy of this exchange is remarkable — the entire awkwardness of Jim's new situation with Charles is compressed into a few words. 'After you' / 'No, I'm staying' / 'Okay' captures the new power dynamic perfectly. Not a big laugh but a precise cringe comedy beat.

jokes.text: Dwight offers to translate the German copier instructions; Pam declines; Dwight invokes American arrogance leading to wars; Pam says 'That's a really—'; Dwight cuts in: 'World War II.'
jokes.setup: Pam is setting up the new copier without reading the (German) instructions
jokes.punchline: Dwight calls out 'typical American arrogance' for not using German instructions — then escalates to 'a war we never should have been in' — which turns out to be World War II (i.e., Germany's war of choice, which America was arguably morally obligated to join)
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight joke. The reveal that his 'war we shouldn't have been in' is WWII — implying he has pro-German sympathies, consistent with his Pennsylvania German heritage and authoritarian personality — is exactly right. Pam's cut-off reaction sells it. High character integration: this joke belongs exclusively to Dwight.

jokes.text: 'That is either an incense dispenser or a ceremonial sarcophagus. My German is preindustrial and mostly religious.'
jokes.setup: Pam asks what a copier part is supposed to do after Dwight reads the German instructions
jokes.punchline: Dwight's two guesses (incense dispenser / ceremonial sarcophagus) and his caveat that his German is 'preindustrial and mostly religious'
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. 'My German is preindustrial and mostly religious' is one of the most perfectly constructed character lines in the series. Every word earns its place: 'preindustrial' (Dwight's identity is rooted in agrarian, anachronistic life), 'mostly religious' (he has a reverent, quasi-theocratic worldview). The two guesses — 'incense dispenser' and 'ceremonial sarcophagus' — are both absurdly theological and exactly wrong for a copier part. This is the joke against which this episode's 9s are measured. Exceptionally original, textbook economy, and exclusively Dwight.

jokes.text: Michael asks Pam to modify the Dunder Mifflin order form to say 'Michael Scott Paper Company' — 'Somebody's been talking in bed. Pillow talk.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks Pam to help rebrand official company forms for his startup
jokes.punchline: 'Somebody's been talking in bed. Pillow talk.' — Michael reacts to Pam knowing about his company idea as if it's gossip from a romantic affair
jokes.explanation: Decent Michael non-sequitur. 'Pillow talk' implies intimacy, which is tonally absurd in this context and slightly creepy — a reliable Michael register. Not the sharpest joke in the episode but it lands.

jokes.text: 'This is a dream that I have had since lunch, and I am not giving up on it now.'
jokes.setup: Jim presses Michael on whether he's really thought this through — it's a 'pretty big risk'
jokes.punchline: Michael insists he won't give up on a dream 'since lunch' — revealing the plan is hours old and presented with the gravity of a lifelong passion
jokes.explanation: Co-equal with joke #25 as the episode's best line. 'A dream I have had since lunch' is a near-perfect joke: the gap between the gravitas of 'a dream I have had' (implying years of longing) and 'since lunch' (approximately two hours) is maximally absurd. It's also deeply character-true — Michael forms monumental emotional attachments to ideas instantly. Perfect economy: the joke is entirely in the juxtaposition of two phrases. Highly quotable, standalone funny, and reveals character. This is an 8-anchor-level joke or better.

jokes.text: Michael's solution to rebranding forms: 'Could I take a piece of paper and just tape it with transparent tape?' / 'Yeah. Good.'
jokes.setup: Pam explains the technical process (scan, upload, copy new image) for modifying the order form header
jokes.punchline: Michael ignores all of it and asks if he can just tape paper over the logo — Pam's defeated 'Yeah. Good.' is the kicker
jokes.explanation: Great Michael joke. The 'tape a piece of paper over it' solution is hilariously on-brand — why use a technical solution when grade-school craft will do? Pam's 'Yeah. Good.' captures exactly the deflation of anyone who has tried to explain technology to someone who won't engage with it.

jokes.text: Angela barges into Michael's office mid-interview to push an accounting seminar — mentions a sundae bar, then: 'I mean, I didn't have any. To stay trim.'
jokes.setup: Charles is conducting a job interview; Angela interrupts with an irrelevant seminar brochure
jokes.punchline: Angela derails a formal meeting to mention a sundae bar at a conference, then feels compelled to clarify she didn't eat any — to stay trim — an unprompted, image-conscious non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: An excellent Angela character beat. The sundae bar confession followed by 'I didn't have any — to stay trim' is a perfect character joke: Angela is simultaneously trying to impress a man and maintain her prim self-image, even in a completely inappropriate moment. The non-sequitur interruption is cringe-funny.

jokes.text: 'Did Michael just let anybody in his office?' / 'Yes. He loved to facilitate communication... He was like, Come in.' / 'I am aware of the effect I have on women.'
jokes.setup: Charles is baffled that Angela interrupted his meeting; Jim explains that Michael had an open-door policy
jokes.punchline: Cut to (implied) Michael talking-head: 'I am aware of the effect I have on women' — Michael interprets Angela's obvious brown-nosing as attraction to him
jokes.explanation: Michael's talking-head — 'I am aware of the effect I have on women' — is delivered with complete earnestness, which makes it funnier. Angela was clearly doing professional networking, and Michael reads it as romantic interest. His delusional self-image collides perfectly with the reality we just witnessed.

jokes.text: 'She's such a special person. She's turning 50 this year.'
jokes.setup: Michael comments on Angela after she leaves
jokes.punchline: Calling Angela 'special' then immediately noting she's 'turning 50 this year' — as if this explains or qualifies the compliment in some way Michael finds meaningful
jokes.explanation: Minor character beat. Michael's non-sequitur age observation is mildly amusing but a step down from the stronger material around it. The connection between 'special' and '50 this year' is left cryptic enough to be slightly funny but not genuinely surprising.

jokes.text: Michael pitches his paper company to the salespeople with theatrical seriousness: 'It's going to be worldwide.'
jokes.setup: Michael approaches salespeople to recruit them to his startup company
jokes.punchline: 'It's going to be worldwide' — Michael's company plan extends from 'I had this idea since lunch' to global domination within minutes
jokes.explanation: Functions mainly as a callback and escalation on the 'dream since lunch' joke. Michael's global ambitions for a company that doesn't yet exist are funny in the context of what we know, but the line itself isn't especially crafted.

jokes.text: 'Well, it's a very intriguing concept, isn't it?' — Dwight's non-committal talking-head about Michael's company
jokes.setup: Michael pitches Dwight on joining the Michael Scott Paper Company
jokes.punchline: Dwight's talking-head is pure diplomatic non-answer — 'isn't it?' deflects any actual position while implying he's considering it seriously
jokes.explanation: Mild beat. The non-answer from someone who is typically dogmatically decisive is a small inversion, but the joke is soft. Functions mainly to show Dwight's conflict.

jokes.text: Multiple confessionals where coworkers are asked about Michael's paper company idea — Jim's deadpan: 'Your own paper company?' (as if it's the most reasonable thing).
jokes.setup: A talking-head sequence where various staff weigh in on Michael starting a rival paper company while still employed by Dunder Mifflin.
jokes.punchline: Jim's completely neutral, inquisitive 'Your own paper company?' — delivered without any of the mock-enthusiasm or sarcasm the audience expects — functions as pure reaction comedy.
jokes.explanation: Jim's camera look and neutral repeat of the premise is a classic mockumentary reaction beat. Not original, but well-executed.

jokes.text: Michael pitches Andy and an unnamed colleague — everyone responds with vague, non-committal enthusiasm ('Lots of potential. Yes. What a courageous venture.')
jokes.setup: Michael pitches his company idea with excitement
jokes.punchline: The responses are all technically positive but completely empty — 'courageous' being the most damning ('brave of you to try this doomed thing')
jokes.explanation: 'What a courageous venture' is the best word in this sequence — 'courageous' in response to a business plan implies they think it will fail spectacularly. Functional cringe comedy as the office collectively humors Michael.

jokes.text: Michael and Dwight talk over each other in excited agreement about farm logistics, neither listening — 'Let's put a pin in it.'
jokes.setup: Dwight raises logistical concerns about his farm obligations; Michael keeps saying 'that's what I was thinking'
jokes.punchline: Both enthusiastically talk past each other, agreeing without hearing — the 'pin in it' suggests they've resolved nothing and both know it
jokes.explanation: A character texture moment more than a structured joke. The mutual non-listening is realistic cringe but not the show's sharpest writing.

jokes.text: 'Little Miss Thing wants attention.' — Meredith's reaction to Michael calling a meeting
jokes.setup: Michael calls for everyone's attention in his final days
jokes.punchline: Meredith's withering 'Little Miss Thing' dismissal of Michael — a grown man being called 'Miss Thing' — is darkly affectionate
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-delivered Meredith line. The phrase 'Little Miss Thing' applied to Michael is incongruously affectionate/dismissive and works as a character moment. Economy is strong: three words, full characterization of Meredith's relationship to Michael.

jokes.text: Michael's farewell announcement turns out to be a bingo game — 'G-44'
jokes.setup: Michael grandly announces 'this is the moment you've all been waiting for' — suggesting an emotional farewell speech
jokes.punchline: He starts calling bingo numbers
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection. The dramatic buildup ('this is the moment you've all been waiting for') invites expectation of an emotional farewell, then subverts it completely with 'G-44.' This captures Michael's emotional imprecision perfectly — he thinks bingo is a meaningful communal activity equivalent to a goodbye speech. The setup/payoff timing is sharp; the payoff lands without explanation.

jokes.text: 'It's not ready, Kevin!'
jokes.setup: Copier has been a recurring source of frustration; Kevin presumably goes back to Pam immediately after she told him 'soon'
jokes.punchline: Pam's exasperated outburst confirms Kevin came right back — 'soon' did not mean now
jokes.explanation: Payoff on the running copier gag. Kevin clearly interpreted 'come back soon' as license to return immediately, which is good character work. The exasperation reads well. Efficient callback.

jokes.text: Pam on the copier: 'I have sunk four hours into that copier. And I am not going to let it beat me like that wireless router did.'
jokes.setup: Pam has been struggling to set up the copier all day
jokes.punchline: The wireless router aside — implying the router won their previous battle — makes her tech failures a running personal narrative of defeat
jokes.explanation: Charming Pam line. 'I am not going to let it beat me like that wireless router did' implies the router definitively won, which is both specific and funny. The competitive framing of tech troubleshooting as personal combat is a good comedic register for Pam.

jokes.text: 'You put a note in my food?' / 'I made it sterile.' / 'Just saying sterile doesn't make it so.'
jokes.setup: Michael left a recruitment note in Oscar's lunch
jokes.punchline: Michael defends note-in-food by claiming he 'made it sterile' — as if that's the problem, and as if that's even possible
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Michael's defense is that he made the paper sterile — completely missing that the violation is the invasion of privacy, not the hygiene. Oscar's 'just saying sterile doesn't make it so' is a perfectly measured put-down. Both characters are exactly themselves.

jokes.text: Oscar's business-plan reality check: 'Best-case scenario, you don't cut yourself a salary for at least five years.' / 'You already have the job. You don't have to convince me.'
jokes.setup: Oscar delivers a comprehensive analysis of why the company can't work
jokes.punchline: Michael, unable to process the critique, tells Oscar he 'already has the job' — treating devastating analysis as enthusiastic acceptance
jokes.explanation: Excellent Michael delusion joke. Oscar's exhaustive case against the company is treated by Michael as a sales pitch being dismissed — he cuts Oscar off before the verdict with 'you already have the job.' The inversion (analysis = rejection vs. Michael's reading: analysis = enthusiasm) is perfectly constructed and character-specific.

jokes.text: Michael interrupts Stanley at a urinal: 'Can't you see I'm urinating?'
jokes.setup: Michael is desperately recruiting employees for his company; he tracks Stanley to the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Stanley's matter-of-fact 'Can't you see I'm urinating?' — he is entirely unimpressed and unbothered by Michael's desperation
jokes.explanation: Very good Stanley line. The delivery of 'Can't you see I'm urinating?' with maximum dignity while at a urinal is peak Stanley — he is too proud and too unbothered to even be embarrassed. The economy is perfect; Stanley's entire character is in this one line.

jokes.text: Stanley in the bathroom: 'Can't you see I'm urinating?'
jokes.setup: Michael has followed Stanley into the bathroom to pitch the paper company. Stanley is mid-urination.
jokes.punchline: Stanley's complete non-surprise at Michael's intrusion — he's annoyed but not shocked — implies this isn't even the first time.
jokes.explanation: Stanley's flat 'Can't you see I'm urinating?' has the cadence of someone who has rehearsed every variation of 'leave me alone' for deployment against Michael. Stanley's long-suffering dignity is a reliable comedy engine. The bathroom pitch is an escalation of Michael's desperation.

jokes.text: 'I want you to think about it.' / 'No.' / 'Okay, you're not letting me finish.' / 'And you just lost out on a million dollars.' / 'No, I didn't.'
jokes.setup: Michael pitches Stanley, who says no before Michael can even make his case
jokes.punchline: 'You just lost out on a million dollars.' — Stanley's immediate 'No, I didn't.' is the perfect refusal to engage with Michael's fantasy valuation
jokes.explanation: Stanley at his best. The rapid-fire 'No.' / 'No, I didn't.' is textbook Stanley: maximum refusal, minimum words. 'No, I didn't' is the ideal punchline because it dismisses Michael's million-dollar claim without even engaging with its absurdity — Stanley simply knows it's false. Sharp economy, perfect character.

jokes.text: 'I had a great time at prom. And no one said yes to that, either.'
jokes.setup: Everyone has rejected Michael's pitch; he tries to spin this as okay
jokes.punchline: Michael's prom analogy inadvertently reveals he went to prom alone (or was rejected by his date) — and reframes universal rejection as a personal positive
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The prom line does multiple things simultaneously: (1) it recontextualizes Michael's current rejection as part of a lifelong pattern, (2) it reveals he went to prom despite universal rejection, which is both sad and admirable, and (3) 'and no one said yes to that, either' implies he still had a great time — which is the most Michael Scott thing possible. The joke lands on pathos and comedy simultaneously. High originality, perfect economy.

jokes.text: Pam's copier victory speech: 'I did it. I learned everything about this machine. I know all the buttons. Even the inside ones. I know all the error messages. I could do a bound book in plastic with offset colors, which feels...'
jokes.setup: After hours of struggle, Pam has finally figured out the new copier
jokes.punchline: Pam's escalating technical mastery speech trails off mid-sentence — implying she's overcome with emotion about a photocopier
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the copier subplot. Pam's pride in 'the inside buttons' and the speech that dies of emotion is a nice character beat — and dramatically ironic, since she's about to abandon the copier she just mastered to join Michael's company. The trailing-off sells the joke. Rewatch bonus is high because the irony deepens on second viewing.

jokes.text: Michael claims 'immunity' for his last two weeks; Charles says not if he's starting a competing company; Michael calls 'Hank' to escort Charles from the building
jokes.setup: Charles catches Michael trying to take company property and orders him out
jokes.punchline: Michael invokes 'immunity' (like a reality show) and then — impossibly — calls Hank the security guard to remove his own boss from the building
jokes.explanation: Escalating audacity joke. Michael invoking 'immunity' is funny enough, but calling Hank to remove his own boss from the building is an absurdist power move that works because of its absolute commitment. The fact that Hank briefly complies ('Come on, man, let's go') makes it even funnier — before presumably stopping.

jokes.text: 'I always thought Michael got a bad rap. He's a good guy. And he's super funny.' / 'Yeah, maybe I should tell him before he goes.' / 'He's all the way over there.'
jokes.setup: Hank's talking-head reveals he actually likes Michael
jokes.punchline: Hank's reason for not telling Michael he likes him: 'He's all the way over there' — implying a modest physical distance is prohibitive
jokes.explanation: Excellent minor-character joke. Hank's 'he's all the way over there' is a beautifully lazy excuse — he's the security guard, crossing the building is his job — and it perfectly captures the show's theme of missed connections due to inertia. The deadpan is perfect. Surprisingly quotable for a throwaway.

jokes.text: Michael's dramatic exit from the office — apparently singing/performing — coworkers watch confused: 'What is he doing?' / 'I think he's singing.'
jokes.setup: Michael has been kicked out and makes his exit from the office building
jokes.punchline: His exit is so theatrical that onlookers aren't sure what they're watching — apparently singing, possibly dancing
jokes.explanation: Strong visual/physical comedy moment. The confusion about what Michael is doing (is he singing? dancing? both?) is funny in itself, and 'I feel free!' lands as a character statement — Michael performing liberation for an audience that isn't sure what he's performing. The mockumentary framing of confused coworkers watching through the window adds layers.

jokes.text: Michael: 'And I feel free!' — sung in the parking lot.
jokes.setup: Michael has been forced out of the building. The staff watch him go.
jokes.punchline: He's singing a dramatic declaration of freedom in the parking lot of his former employer, alone, in the middle of the day.
jokes.explanation: Michael's theatrical self-narration is consistent with his character. The absurdity of singing 'I feel free' in a Scranton parking lot while being watched by former employees is the image. Works as part of the exit sequence rather than a standalone.

jokes.text: 'And just like that, as mysteriously as he arrived, he was gone.'
jokes.setup: Michael makes his exit
jokes.punchline: Dwight's narrator-voice talking-head treats Michael's departure as the end of a fairy tale or myth — 'as mysteriously as he arrived'
jokes.explanation: Lovely Dwight talking-head. The mythological framing — 'as mysteriously as he arrived' — is both ridiculous (Michael's arrival is documented employment history) and touching (Dwight genuinely sees Michael as a mysterious, larger-than-life figure). The cadence is that of closing narration, which makes it funnier and more affecting simultaneously.

jokes.text: 'The whole office feels darker. You know? It's just a sad, dark day.'
jokes.setup: Michael has left; Andy gives his reaction
jokes.punchline: Andy's overwrought eulogizing of Michael's departure as a 'sad, dark day' — Andy who sucked up to Michael compulsively now doesn't know what to do with himself
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat. Andy's grief is in character given his sycophantic relationship to Michael, but the line itself isn't especially sharp. Mostly setup for the next beat.

jokes.text: 'Andy, he's gone. You don't have to kiss his ass anymore.'
jokes.setup: Andy is dramatically mourning Michael's departure
jokes.punchline: Jim points out that Andy's grief is likely habit — he doesn't need to perform devotion anymore
jokes.explanation: Sharp Jim line. The implication that Andy's grief might be pure muscle memory from years of sycophancy is a good character insight delivered efficiently. 'You don't have to kiss his ass anymore' is blunt and funny.

jokes.text: 'Michael's like a movie on a plane. You know, it's not great, but it's something to watch. And then when it's over, you're like, how much time is left on this flight? You know. Now what?'
jokes.setup: Michael is gone; Jim gives his talking-head assessment
jokes.punchline: The plane-movie metaphor — not great but essential — perfectly captures Michael's role in the office ecosystem
jokes.explanation: The episode's finest talking-head and one of the best Jim lines in the series. The plane-movie analogy is original, structural perfect, and devastatingly true about Michael Scott. It works on three levels: (1) as a joke about Michael specifically, (2) as an observation about how we rely on distraction to survive tedium, and (3) as an emotionally honest admission that Jim will miss something he didn't value. 'Now what?' as the final two words is a perfect kicker — both funny and genuinely sad. This is premium comedy writing.

jokes.text: 'Michael? Don't look down. Look straight up.'
jokes.setup: Michael is apparently crawling on the floor to avoid being seen by Charles on the way back to recruit more people
jokes.punchline: 'Don't look down. Look straight up.' implies Michael is crawling below desk level — a grown man army-crawling through an office
jokes.explanation: Strong implied physical comedy. 'Don't look down. Look straight up' is a genuinely funny directorial instruction for crawling — Michael is giving guidance for where to position his eyeline while on hands and knees in the office. The visual is inherently funny and the line captures it efficiently.

jokes.text: Jim: 'I did have a chance to think about it, but then I thought about something else. So, which way are you leaning?' / Michael: 'Well, it is tempting, but I am 100% leaning towards passing.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks Jim if he's thought about the offer to join his company
jokes.punchline: Jim confirms he thought about it briefly, then thought about something else — and is '100% leaning towards passing'
jokes.explanation: Solid Jim-Michael exchange. 'I thought about it, but then I thought about something else' is a perfectly casual brush-off, and 'I am tempting, but 100% leaning towards passing' has the right deadpan diplomatic register — honoring Michael's pitch while completely rejecting it.

jokes.text: Michael crawling back in, coaching employees on where to look while he's on the floor: 'Don't look at me. People, stop. Don't look down. Don't look down. He's gonna see me.'
jokes.setup: Michael has snuck back into the office to recruit more staff while supposedly banned by Charles
jokes.punchline: Michael is visibly crawling and directing employees' gaze as if this is a viable stealth strategy
jokes.explanation: The crawling bit escalates nicely. Michael's elaborate stealth coaching ('not all the way up — keep them at a normal height') reveals he has a detailed strategy for this that makes no sense. The physical comedy here would be very strong on screen.

jokes.text: 'This is not Michael Scott talking right now. This is your future. Hello. I am your future. You are older and you are very happy now, because you went with Michael Scott, right?'
jokes.setup: Michael, crawling, attempts a motivational speech to get employees to join him
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'I am your future' speech is delivered from the floor, positing himself as a time traveler from a better tomorrow — while crawling
jokes.explanation: Excellent Michael absurdist moment. The 'I am your future' conceit — delivered while crawling on an office floor — is beautifully self-undermining. The follow-up 'You are older and very happy because you went with Michael Scott, right?' turns it into a question, destroying the prophecy's authority. High character integration: Michael's grandiosity knows no physical circumstances.

jokes.text: Michael's call to action: 'Are you being the best that you can be? All right, everybody who's gonna go with me, I want you to stomp your foot.'
jokes.setup: Michael is still on the floor trying to recruit colleagues
jokes.punchline: Asking people to 'stomp their foot' as a voting mechanism — as if foot-stomping constitutes a binding commitment — then waiting as nobody does
jokes.explanation: Good escalation on the floor-crawling absurdity. Michael converts a stealth recruiting visit into a revival-meeting style call-and-response, demanding foot stomps. The gap between what Michael needs to accomplish and his chosen method is funny.

jokes.text: Charles vs. Michael standoff — Michael: 'I've got nothing to lose.' / Charles: 'Okay.' / Michael: 'Oh, my God. No, God! No! No. All right. It's not worth it.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Charles face off; Michael declares he has 'nothing to lose'
jokes.punchline: Whatever Charles does (presumably steps toward him), Michael immediately folds — 'No, God! No. It's not worth it' — his bold talk evaporates instantly
jokes.explanation: Great cringe payoff. Michael's bravado collapses at the first sign of physical threat — 'No, God! No!' is a genuinely funny panic. The contrast between 'I've got nothing to lose' and 'it's not worth it' ten seconds later is the entire joke. Charles doesn't even need to say anything; his presence alone defeats Michael.

jokes.text: Pam announces she's going with Michael — 'I'm going!' — to everyone's shock
jokes.setup: Michael has failed to recruit anyone; the situation seems totally defeated
jokes.punchline: Pam — who earlier said quitting was a dream she'd never achieve — stands up and declares she's going with Michael
jokes.explanation: The episode's biggest narrative payoff. The callback to Pam's 'but I dream' talking-head makes this moment both funny and genuinely moving. The joke is in the shock/misdirection — nobody expected her to do it — but it's also earned through everything we know about Pam's character. High craft because it delivers on a joke set up 18 minutes earlier. 'I'm going!' is simple but the delivery and context make it explosive.

jokes.text: Pam decides to quit and join Michael: 'I'm going with him.' / 'What? Pam.' / 'I'm going!'
jokes.setup: The episode has established Pam as the sensible, stable presence. Michael has been rejected by everyone.
jokes.punchline: Pam — of all people — is the one who quits to join Michael. The complete subversion of expectations (she's the last person anyone would expect) is the comedy, alongside Jim's helpless 'What? Pam.'
jokes.explanation: A strong structural surprise. The episode has carefully shown everyone rejecting Michael, making Pam's impulsive leap genuinely shocking. It's also good character development — Pam's desire to escape the receptionist job has been building. Jim's helpless 'What? Pam.' is an excellent straight-man reaction. High impact because of the genuine surprise factor.

jokes.text: Pam's negotiation: 'Except I don't want to be a receptionist anymore.' / 'Executive assistant.' / 'Salesman.' / 'All right. Okay.' / 'Deal.'
jokes.setup: Pam agrees to join Michael but immediately starts negotiating
jokes.punchline: Pam's rapid job-title negotiation — jumping from 'not receptionist' to 'executive assistant' to 'salesman' in seconds — and Michael immediately agreeing without consideration
jokes.explanation: Excellent scene. The joke is in the negotiation's absurdity (she's bargaining about titles at a company with no clients, no office, and no salary) and Michael's complete willingness to grant any title. 'Salesman' / 'All right. Okay.' / 'Deal.' is a rapid-fire exchange that captures both Pam's new assertiveness and Michael's complete lack of business sense. Very funny and character-revealing.

jokes.text: 'Michael, it's not how you leave an office. It's how you—' / 'Jim, Jim, Jim. We're having a company meeting here.'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to give Michael advice about how to make a dignified exit; Pam points out all his stuff is still upstairs
jokes.punchline: Michael cuts Jim off with 'We're having a company meeting here' — declaring a two-person sidewalk huddle a formal company meeting
jokes.explanation: Strong Michael closer. Designating a sidewalk conversation between two people as a 'company meeting' is absurdist but also revealing — Michael is already fully in his new role, treating himself as a functioning CEO. The delivery of 'Jim, Jim, Jim' as a dismissal of wisdom is also very on-brand.

jokes.text: Charles's solution to losing the receptionist: Kevin on phones, Stanley as 'productivity czar'
jokes.setup: Charles must reorganize the office now that both Michael and Pam have left
jokes.punchline: He appoints Kevin — the least phone-capable person — to phones, and Stanley — the least productive person — as 'productivity czar'
jokes.explanation: Excellent closing joke. The irony is perfectly deployed: Charles, who presents himself as a decisive, competent manager, immediately assigns the two worst people to the two most critical roles. Kevin on phones is bad enough; Stanley as 'productivity czar' — a man who does crossword puzzles at his desk — is inspired. High character integration because the comedy depends on knowing exactly what Kevin and Stanley are like. Good button for the episode.

tmdb_overview: Michael's relationship with the new vice president becomes increasingly tense, as Michael finds an excuse to goof off even more than usual. Meanwhile, Pam faces the challenge of a new copier and Kelly develops a crush.
